text: Orvanta protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of customer funds records, payment services and personal data, and meets its legal, regulatory and contractual duties.
The Management Board approves this policy, and the CEO communicates it to all staff and relevant suppliers.
Security objectives are set each year in the ISMS Manual (ORV-ISMS-001), measured monthly and reported to the Management Board every quarter.
Risks are assessed and treated under the Risk Management Methodology (ORV-RISK-001), and selected controls are recorded in the Statement of Applicability.
The CISO reports to the CEO and may raise any risk directly with the Management Board.
Every system, data class, supplier and control has a named owner, recorded in the asset register or the Statement of Applicability.
Conflicting duties are separated. Where a small team makes that impractical, the CISO approves a compensating control such as independent review.
Managers explain security duties to their teams, check that training is completed and act on policy breaches.
The Head of Compliance keeps current contacts for the Bank of Lithuania, the State Data Protection Inspectorate and the national CSIRT.
The CISO keeps Orvanta in at least one financial-sector security information sharing group.
The CISO reviews threat intelligence every month and updates the threat catalog and detection rules.
Projects that change systems or data handling include a security check at the start and before launch.
The Head of Compliance maintains a register of legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, each with an owner.
Software and content are used within their license terms, and open-source licenses are checked in CI.
Records are kept and deleted according to the retention schedule owned by the Head of Compliance.
Personal data is handled as the DPO directs, including transfer safeguards for access from Baku.
The ISMS is reviewed independently every year through the internal audit programme.
Control owners test their controls on the calendar set by the CISO and keep the evidence.
Security-relevant operating procedures are documented, owned and kept in the controlled ISMS space in Confluence.
Each office has a defined perimeter, with badge or reception-controlled entry and a visitor log.
Offices are locked out of hours, and entrances are monitored by CCTV or the landlord's equivalent, confirmed yearly.
Production runs only in AWS. The CISO reviews AWS assurance reports every year for physical, environmental and utility protection.
No office holds production systems, so Orvanta has no secure areas. If that changes, the CISO sets rules before the systems arrive.
Office network equipment sits in locked cabinets with protected cabling, and only IT Operations or approved suppliers maintain it.
Access is granted by role, on least privilege and need to know, and approved by the system owner.
Every person has one named identity in Okta. Shared accounts are not allowed.
Each service account has a named owner, no interactive login and credentials held in AWS Secrets Manager.
All workforce applications sign in through Okta single sign-on with MFA. An application that cannot do so is retired or covered by an approved exception.
Administrators authenticate with phishing-resistant security keys.
Passwords are at least 14 characters, unique to each service and stored in the company password manager.
Long-lived cloud access keys are not allowed in repositories or on laptops. Pipelines use short-lived OIDC roles.
Privileged access to AWS, Kubernetes and databases is requested just in time, approved, time-limited and logged.
Standing administrators are limited to two Okta super admins and one sealed break-glass account, which is tested every quarter.
Administrative tools such as kubectl and database clients are limited to approved roles, and their sessions are recorded.
Access to production personal data is restricted by role, masked by default and time-limited for support cases.
Source code access is granted by repository team, and production repositories have branch protection.
Joiner, mover and leaver changes follow the User Access Procedure (ORV-PRC-01). Leaver access is removed within 24 hours of the last working day.
System owners review access every quarter, and privileged access is reviewed every month.
Production networks are private, defined in Terraform and reached only through identity-aware access. Shared VPN profiles are not allowed.
Required security settings for network services, such as Cloudflare and AWS load balancers, are documented and checked in code review.
Production, staging, development and legacy environments run in separate AWS accounts with restricted connections between them.
Company systems are for business use. Limited personal use is allowed when it is lawful and adds no security risk.
Every user acknowledges this policy when joining and once a year.

Company information is stored only in approved tools: Google Workspace, Confluence, Jira, GitHub, Slack and the business systems. Personal email and personal cloud storage are not used for company information.
Credentials, card numbers and customer identity documents are never placed in Slack, tickets, email or code.
Users do not install unlicensed software, disable security tools or connect unapproved devices.
Customer data, cardholder data and other Restricted information are not entered into external AI tools without CISO approval.
Orvanta monitors its systems for security purposes within the law, and tells users how.
Screens lock after five minutes of inactivity, and users lock their device whenever they leave it.
Desks, printers and whiteboards are cleared of confidential information at the end of the day.
Web access from company devices is filtered for malicious sites, and users do not bypass the filter.
Users report suspected incidents, phishing and lost devices at once through the #security-report channel or the phishing report button.
IT Operations keeps one asset register covering systems, devices, SaaS tools, data classes and supplier services, each with a named owner.
The register is reconciled every month against Terraform, Jamf and Okta.
Leavers return all assets by their last working day, and IT Operations records the return.
Owners classify information as Public, Internal, Confidential or Restricted.
Restricted information, meaning cardholder data, identity documents and credentials, is stored only in systems approved for it.
Documents and shared drives holding Confidential or Restricted information carry a label.
Confidential and Restricted information leaves Orvanta only through approved channels, under contract and encrypted.
Access to personal data from outside the EEA, including from Baku, follows the transfer impact assessment approved by the DPO.
Information is deleted at the end of its retention period, automatically where the system allows.
Full card numbers are not stored in any Orvanta system. Support tickets are redacted automatically and searched every month.
Personal data is masked by default in reporting, support views and non-production environments.
Data loss prevention rules alert on bulk exports and on external sharing of Confidential and Restricted information.
Removable storage is blocked on the devices of roles that handle Restricted information.
Devices are wiped, with evidence, before reuse. Disposal goes through a supplier that issues a destruction certificate.
Production data at rest is encrypted with keys managed in AWS KMS.
Data in transit uses TLS 1.2 or higher, including traffic between internal services.
Laptop disks are encrypted with FileVault, enforced through Jamf.
Backups are encrypted with keys held in the backup account.
Only approved algorithms and managed cryptographic services are used. Teams do not design their own cryptography.
Card data cryptography stays with Tessarin. Orvanta systems handle tokens and truncated card numbers only.
Keys and secrets are created and stored in AWS KMS or Secrets Manager, never in code, tickets or chat.
Each key has an owner, a purpose and a rotation date in the key inventory.
KMS keys rotate every year. Secrets and SFTP keys rotate at least every year, and immediately after suspected exposure.
Access to keys is limited by role and logged in CloudTrail.
Certificates are issued and renewed automatically, and expiry is monitored.
Changes follow the secure development life cycle, with security gates set by the risk tier of the change.
Security requirements, including abuse cases, are written for changes to payment, account and card functions.
Major design changes go through threat modeling against the published engineering principles.
All code is peer reviewed. Static analysis, dependency scanning and secret scanning run in every pipeline.
Security tests run before release: dynamic testing in staging for web and API changes, and a penetration test every year.
Orvanta does not outsource development today. If that changes, this policy and its reviews apply by contract.
Development, staging and production run in separate AWS accounts, and engineers hold no standing production access.
Live personal data is not used in development or staging. Test data is synthetic or masked.
Production changes deploy only through the CI pipeline, from protected branches, with approval from a second person.
Emergency changes use the logged break-glass route and are reviewed within two working days.
Infrastructure is defined in Terraform and applied only from CI. Configuration drift raises an alert.
Software reaches production only as built images. Manual installs on production hosts are not allowed.
Vulnerabilities are handled under the Vulnerability and Patch Management Procedure (ORV-PRC-02): critical within 7 days, high within 30, medium within 90.
Third-party components are tracked in a software bill of materials generated in CI.
Audit and penetration tests on production are scoped and scheduled with the Head of Platform and SRE to avoid disruption.
Every supplier that handles Orvanta information or supports a critical service is recorded, tiered and given an owner.
Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers pass a security assessment before a contract is signed and before any data is shared.
Contracts include security, confidentiality, incident notification, audit, subprocessor and exit clauses, using the contract checklist.
Suppliers disclose their subprocessors, and Tier 1 suppliers show how they manage their own supply chain.
ICT suppliers that support critical or important functions are recorded in the DORA register of information.
Supplier access to Orvanta systems is named, protected by MFA, limited to the task and removed when the contract ends.
Tier 1 suppliers are reviewed every year and Tier 2 every two years. Assurance reports are tracked for expiry.
A significant change or incident at a supplier triggers a reassessment.
Cloud services follow the cloud security standard, which includes a shared responsibility matrix and exit considerations.
Supplier incidents that affect Orvanta are handled under the Incident Management Policy.
At the end of a contract, the supplier returns or destroys Orvanta information and confirms it in writing.
The CISO maintains the incident response plan, the on-call rota and playbooks for ransomware and cloud credential compromise.
The plan is exercised at least once a year through a tabletop exercise, and lessons update the playbooks.
Staff and suppliers report suspected security events immediately through #security-report or the on-call number.
Events are triaged against the severity matrix. Severity 1 and 2 events are declared incidents.
Each incident has one incident lead with authority to isolate systems and revoke access.
The Head of Compliance and the DPO join any incident that may need regulatory or customer notification. Deadlines follow the notification matrix.
The CEO or a named delegate approves communication with customers, regulators and the media.
Incident records are kept in the restricted security project in Jira.
Evidence is preserved under the evidence handling procedure, with chain of custody, before systems are rebuilt.
Severity 1 and 2 incidents get a post-incident review within 10 working days. Actions are tracked to closure and feed the risk register.
Production databases and document stores are backed up at least daily. The ledger also has point-in-time recovery.
Backups are copied to a separate AWS account with immutability, and to a second EU region.
No single identity can delete both production data and its backups.
Backup jobs are monitored, and a failure alerts the on-call engineer.
Backups are kept for the periods in the retention schedule.
Important SaaS data, including GitHub and Google Workspace, has an export or backup arrangement.
A full restore of each critical database is tested every quarter, and the result is recorded.
Recovery time and recovery point objectives for each critical service come from the Business Impact Analysis and are approved by the COO.
Critical services run across at least three availability zones.
Continuity plans exist for critical processes and are exercised every year.
Security controls stay in force during a disruption. Any emergency relaxation is approved by the CISO, logged and reversed afterwards.
Audit logging is enabled in every AWS account and for Okta, GitHub and Google Workspace.
Logs are sent to a central log account that workload administrators cannot change.
Security logs are kept for at least 12 months.
Logs do not contain secrets, full card numbers or personal data that is not needed.
All systems take time from AWS time synchronization or an equivalent trusted source.
A SIEM runs detection rules mapped to MITRE ATT&CK for the priority attack scenarios.
Alerts are triaged every working day, and high-severity alerts page the on-call engineer.
Detection coverage is reviewed every quarter against the threat catalog.
Privileged activity and break-glass use are reviewed every month by someone other than the person who acted.
Monitoring follows privacy law, and its purposes are agreed with the DPO.
Capacity and performance are monitored with alerts, and capacity is forecast every year.
Company work is done only on company laptops enrolled in Jamf.
Okta blocks sign-in from devices that are not managed.
Laptops have disk encryption, EDR, automatic updates, screen lock and remote wipe enforced.
EDR alerts go to the SIEM, and users cannot switch the agent off.
Personal phones are used only for Okta Verify, Slack and email, through managed apps.
DNS filtering for malicious sites is active on every laptop.
Remote workers use a private space, keep screens out of view and do not let others use their company device.
Any network may be used, because access goes through encrypted, identity-aware connections. Shared VPN profiles are not used.
Laptops are not left unattended in vehicles or public places, and a loss is reported within one hour.
Work from a country outside the approved list needs approval from the Head of People and the CISO.
Confidential documents are not printed outside the office.
Candidates are screened before they start: identity, right to work and references. Roles with privileged access or control of funds also have criminal record checks where the law allows.
Employment and contractor agreements include confidentiality, security duties and acceptance of the security policies. Vilnius and Baku use aligned templates.
Contractors and other third parties sign a non-disclosure agreement before they see Confidential information.
New joiners complete security induction in their first week, and before they receive production access.
All staff complete security training every year, with role-based modules for engineers, support and finance.
Phishing simulations run every quarter, and people who click repeatedly get coaching.
Policy breaches are handled under the disciplinary process, fairly and in proportion. Reporting in good faith is never penalized.
The Head of People tells IT Operations about leavers and movers on the day the change is confirmed.
Confidentiality duties continue after employment ends, and leavers are reminded of them at exit.
Managers confirm that assets are returned and knowledge is handed over.
